arml-2017-power-01a.title: Test x = O + 1
arml-2017-power-01a.body: The condition says $\min(O,x)=x$ for every $x$. But for $x=O+1$, $\min(O,O+1)=O\ne O+1$. So no such $O$ exists. ∎

arml-2017-power-02.title: Translate
arml-2017-power-02.body: The left side is $a+\min(b,c)$; the right side is $\min(a+b,a+c)$. If $b\le c$, both equal $a+b$; if $b>c$, both equal $a+c$. ∎

arml-2017-power-03a.title: Translate and split
arml-2017-power-03a.body:
The equation is $\min(2x,\,x+2,\,1)=\min(x,2)$.

- If $x<\frac12$: $2x<1$ and $2x<x+2$, so the left side is $2x$, and $x<2$ so the right side is $x$. Then $2x=x$, $x=0$.
- If $x\ge\frac12$: the left side is $1$ (since $2x\ge1$ and $x+2>1$), so $\min(x,2)=1$, $x=1$.

Both check. **Answer: $x=0$ and $x=1$**

arml-2017-power-03b.title: Translate and split
arml-2017-power-03b.body:
The equation is $\min(2x,-1)=\min(x,1)+\min(x,-1)$.

- $x\le-1$: both sides are $2x$ — every such $x$ works.
- $-1<x<-\frac12$: $2x=x-1$ gives $x=-1$, not in the interval.
- $-\frac12\le x\le1$: $-1=x-1$, so $x=0$.
- $x>1$: $-1=1-1=0$, impossible.

**Answer: $x=0$ and all $x\le-1$**

arml-2017-power-04a.title: Translate
arml-2017-power-04a.body: In normal arithmetic $a^{\odot n}=n\cdot a$. So the identity reads $n(x+y)=nx+ny$, the ordinary distributive law. ∎

arml-2017-power-04b.title: Translate
arml-2017-power-04b.body: The identity reads $n\cdot\min(x,y)=\min(nx,ny)$. Since $n>0$, multiplying by $n$ preserves order: if $x\le y$ both sides are $nx$, otherwise both are $ny$. ∎

arml-2017-power-04c.title: Arithmetic mean
arml-2017-power-04c.body: The first equality is part (b) with $n=2$. For the second: the right side is $\min(2x,\,x+y,\,2y)$. Since $x+y$ is the average of $2x$ and $2y$, it is at least the smaller of them, so $\min(2x,x+y,2y)=\min(2x,2y)=x^{\odot2}\oplus y^{\odot2}$. ∎

arml-2017-power-05a.title: Translate
arml-2017-power-05a.body: $x^{\odot2}=x+x=2x$, so the equation is $2x=a$, with the unique solution $x=\frac a2$. ∎

arml-2017-power-05b.title: Translate
arml-2017-power-05b.body: $I=0$ (the only real number with $I+x=x$), so the equation is $a+x=0$, with the unique solution $x=-a$. ∎

arml-2017-power-05c.title: Translate
arml-2017-power-05c.body: By parts (a) and (b), $\sqrt[\circ]{y}=\frac y2$ and $\hat y=-y$. So the left side is $\frac{-a}{2}$ and the right side is $-\frac a2$; these are equal. ∎

arml-2017-power-06a.title: Example
arml-2017-power-06a.body: $f(x)=(0\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(0\odot x)\oplus1=\min(2x,x,1)$. This is $2x$ for $x\le0$, $x$ for $0<x<1$, and $1$ for $x\ge1$, so it is $0$ only at $x=0$. ∎

arml-2017-power-06b.title: Example
arml-2017-power-06b.body: Yes. $f(x)=(4\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(3\odot x)\oplus(-1)=\min(2x+4,\,x+3,\,-1)\le-1$ for all $x$, so it never equals $0$. ∎

arml-2017-power-06c.title: Example
arml-2017-power-06c.body:
Yes. $f(x)=(0\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(0\odot x)\oplus0=\min(2x,x,0)=0$ for every $x\ge0$.

(In general, $(a\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(b\odot x)\oplus c$ has no roots if $c<0$, infinitely many if $c=0$, and exactly one if $c>0$.) ∎

arml-2017-power-06d.title: Monotonicity
arml-2017-power-06d.body:
In normal arithmetic,
$$f(x)=\min(nx+a_n,\,(n-1)x+a_{n-1},\,\dots,\,x+a_1,\,a_0),$$
a minimum of lines with nonnegative slopes. Each line is nondecreasing, so $f$ is nondecreasing: $x\le y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y)$.

If $r_1<r_2$ are roots, then for every $z\in[r_1,r_2]$, $0=f(r_1)\le f(z)\le f(r_2)=0$, so $f(z)=0$. That's infinitely many roots. ∎

arml-2017-power-07.title: Translate, then translate back
arml-2017-power-07.body:
In normal arithmetic $f(x)=\min(2x+a,\,x+b,\,c)$. For large $x$ (beyond $\max(\frac{c-a}2,c-b)$) $f(x)=c$, and $f(x)\le c$ always; $f$ is nondecreasing. So if $c<0$ there are no roots and if $c=0$ there are infinitely many; exactly one root forces $c>0$.

With $c>0$, $f(x)=0$ means $\min(2x+a,x+b)=0$ (it is below $c$). The function $\min(2x+a,x+b)$ is strictly increasing, and it is $0$ exactly when both $x\ge-\frac a2$ and $x\ge-b$ with equality in one, i.e.
$$x=\max\left(-\tfrac a2,-b\right)=-\min\left(\tfrac a2,b\right).$$
Translating back: $\frac a2=\sqrt[\circ]{a}$, $\min$ is $\oplus$, negation is the parallel reciprocal, so
$$x=\widehat{\left(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b\right)}.$$
Equivalent forms such as $\sqrt[\circ]{\widehat{a\oplus b^{\odot2}}}$ also work. (But $\sqrt[\circ]{\hat a}\oplus\hat b$ does not — it is $\min(-\frac a2,-b)$; reciprocals reverse $\oplus$.) ∎

arml-2017-power-07.title: Parallel-universe verification
arml-2017-power-07.body:
Let $x=\widehat{(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)}$. Using $\widehat{y^{\odot n}}=(\hat y)^{\odot n}$, a common "denominator" $(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)^{\odot 2}$, the distributive law (Problem 2) and Problem 4:
$$f(x)=\Big[a\oplus\big(b\odot\sqrt[\circ]{a}\big)\oplus b^{\odot2}\oplus(c\odot a)\oplus(c\odot b^{\odot2})\Big]\odot\widehat{(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)}^{\odot2}.$$
Since $c>0$, $a\oplus(c\odot a)=a$ and $b^{\odot2}\oplus(c\odot b^{\odot2})=b^{\odot2}$. By Problem 4c the bracket is $(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)^{\odot2}$, so $f(x)=(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)^{\odot2}\odot\widehat{(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)^{\odot2}}=0$. ∎

arml-2017-power-08a.title: Look far to the left
arml-2017-power-08a.body:
Let $g(x)=k\odot(x\oplus r)\odot(x\oplus s)$; by distributivity $g(x)=(k\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(k\odot(r\oplus s)\odot x)\oplus(k\odot r\odot s)$. In normal arithmetic $f(x)=\min(2x+a,x+b,c)$.

For $x<\min(\frac{c-a}2,b-a)$, $f(x)=2x+a$; for $x<r\,(\le s)$, $g(x)=k+2x$. Choosing $x$ below both bounds, $2x+a=2x+k$, so $k=a$. ∎

arml-2017-power-08b.title: Look far to the right
arml-2017-power-08b.body: For $x>\max(\frac{c-a}2,c-b)$, $f(x)=c$. For $x>s\,(\ge r)$, $g(x)=k+r+s=k\odot r\odot s$. Choosing $x$ large enough for both, $c=k\odot r\odot s=a\odot r\odot s$ by part (a). Applying $\odot\hat a$ to both sides gives $r\odot s=c\odot\hat a$. ∎

arml-2017-power-09.title: Two cases
arml-2017-power-09.body:
For a factorization $(k,r,s)$, since $r\le s$ we have $r\oplus s=r$, and by Problem 8, $g(x)=(a\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(a\odot r\odot x)\oplus c$ and $r+s=c-a$. In normal arithmetic, $f(x)=\min(2x+a,x+b,c)$ and $g(x)=\min(2x+a,x+a+r,c)$.

**Case 1: $2b<a+c$** (so $b-a<c-b$). Take $x=\frac{c-a}2$. Then $x<c-b$, so $f(x)=x+b<c$, while $2x+a=c$. So $g(x)\ne c$ forces $g(x)=x+a+r$, and $x+b=x+a+r$ gives $r=b-a$, $s=c-a-r=c-b$. Conversely $(a,b-a,c-b)$ works: then $a\odot r=b$ and $a\odot r\odot s=c$, so $g=f$ term by term.

**Case 2: $2b\ge a+c$** (so $c-b\le b-a$). Every $x$ satisfies $x\le b-a$ (so $2x+a\le x+b$) or $x\ge c-b$ (so $c\le x+b$); hence $f(x)=\min(2x+a,c)$. If $r<c-a-r$, pick $x$ strictly between; then $x+a+r<2x+a$ and $x+a+r<c$, so $g(x)=x+a+r$, which must equal $2x+a$ or $c$ — giving $x=r$ or $x=c-a-r$, a contradiction. So $r\ge\frac{c-a}2$; but $r\le s$ and $r+s=c-a$ give $r\le\frac{c-a}2$. So $r=s=d=\frac{c-a}2$, $k=a$. Conversely, by Problem 4b, $a\odot(x\oplus d)^{\odot2}=(a\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(a\odot d^{\odot2})=(a\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus c=f(x)$.

In each case exactly one factorization exists. ∎
